items.title: Functional brain signatures of successful cognitive aging
items.author: Niklas Behrenbruch, Larissa Fischer, Hans Kirschner, Theresa M. Harrison, Anne Maass
items.content: <article>Cognitive aging trajectories vary markedly. While many older adults experience gradual decline in memory and executive function, some maintain high cognitive performance well into advanced age. Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying this variability carries important implications for early detection of unfavorable aging trajectories and the development of interventions. Here, we review functional brain signatures associated with successful cognitive aging in humans, integrating evidence from functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography within a unified conceptual framework of brain maintenance and compensation. Across both modalities, evidence increasingly links successful cognitive aging to the preservation of youth-like neural dynamics, while the contribution of compensatory neural recruitment remains empirically contested and methodologically difficult to establish.</article>

items.title: Creative cognition in frontotemporal dementia and brain health
items.author: Agustin Ibanez, Aranza Wille-Bille
items.content: <article>Creative cognition is central to human thought and is affected by brain disease. Recent findings by Altmayer and colleagues link creative impairment in frontotemporal dementia to rostral prefrontal functional differentiation. These findings motivate a framework for investigating network coordination, circuit physiology, experience-dependent plasticity, and bodily and social regulation in creativity and health.</article>

items.title: Constructing events across perception, action, and thought
items.author: Dasom Kwon, Jiwoong Park, Won Mok Shim
items.content: <article>The brain organizes continuous experience into events that structure episodic memory and guide behavior. Traditional accounts have primarily focused on sensory discontinuities and prediction errors that trigger updates of event models. Here, we broaden this view to consider event boundaries arising during goal-directed behavior, spontaneous thought, and memory recall, including transitions generated in the absence of corresponding changes in sensory input. We propose that prediction error and uncertainty provide complementary signals for event model updating: prediction errors signal a violation of current expectations, whereas uncertainty may promote updating when upcoming states become difficult to predict. We further suggest that the hippocampus may serve as a candidate hub linking boundary-related representational changes across perception, action, and thought. Together, this framework offers an integrative account of how the brain detects and generates event structure in continuous experience to support memory and behavior.</article>

items.title: Trends at 50: a mission that matters
items.author: The Trends Editorial Team
items.content: <article>What makes a great review article in your field? As more research is published every day, it has become increasingly difficult to keep up with the latest developments and to ensure that you are hearing from the leading scientists driving these innovations and advances. How do you know what is new and what is valuable?</article>

items.title: Mind the route: different routes, different roles in descending motor pathways
items.author: Arjun M. Narayanan, Anupama Sathyamurthy
items.content: <article>How are distinct descending motor pathways specified during development, and how do they contribute to movement? In a recent study, Kaiser et al. identified molecularly distinct cortical projection neurons that establish separate descending trajectories early in development. Their findings reveal a direct cortico-brainstem pathway with a specific role in skilled forelimb control, highlighting how developmental molecular identity can shape the functional organisation of descending motor circuits.</article>

items.title: Evolving perspectives on cardiac innervation: from relay to a complex regulated network
items.author: Beth A. Habecker, Johanna M. Montgomery
items.content: <article>Neural control of the heart adjusts cardiac output to the functional demands of the body in order to maintain homeostasis. Sensory afferents monitor blood pressure, metabolites, and other parameters, sending information to the brainstem that then alters the balance of stimulatory sympathetic and inhibitory parasympathetic transmission to the heart. ‘Autonomic imbalance’ between sympathetic and parasympathetic efferent transmission in the heart is a characteristic of cardiovascular and metabolic diseases that contributes to pathology. In this review, we discuss recent studies related to the peripheral components of the cardiac control circuit. We summarize data from induced pluripotent stem cells, small and large animal models, and human studies that reveal more complexity in peripheral components of this system than previously understood. We also discuss peripheral neuroplasticity in cardiovascular disease and the potential impact of neuromodulation therapies.</article>

items.title: Organization of neuropeptide signaling: cross-species insights from small model organisms
items.author: Meet Zandawala, Alessandro Filosa, Isabel Beets
items.content: <article>Neuropeptides are ancient signaling molecules that modulate neural circuit function and behavior across the animal kingdom. Model organisms such as Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, and zebrafish serve as powerful in vivo models for deciphering the organization of neuropeptidergic signaling, owing to their smaller nervous systems, genetic tractability, and the growing availability of neural connectomes. In this article, we review how these organisms have advanced current understanding of neuropeptidergic transmission across three interconnected themes: (i) the roles of peptides in sensory–motor transformations, (ii) the conservation and divergence of peptidergic expression and network architecture across species, and (iii) the diversity of neurotransmission strategies employed by single neurons. Finally, we highlight recent technological innovations as well as open questions that could shape this field in the coming years.</article>
